Data

Most of the following examples are an analysis of data in the Employee data set, included with lessR. First read the Employee data into the data frame d. See the Read and Write vignette for more details.

d <- Read("Employee")
##

As an option, also read the table of variable labels. Create the table formatted as two columns. The first column is the variable name and the second column is the corresponding variable label. Not all variables need be entered into the table. The table can be a csv file or an Excel file.

Read the label file into the l data frame, currently the only permitted name. The labels will be displayed on both the text and visualization output. Each displayed label is the variable name juxtaposed with the corresponding label, as shown in the following output.

l <- rd("Employee_lbl")

Histogram

One of the most frequently encountered visualizations for continuous variables is the histogram, which outlines the general shape of the underlying distribution.

Histogram: Bin similar values into a group, then plot the frequency of occurrence of the data values in each bin proportional to the height of the corresponding bar.

A call to a function to create a histogram contains the name of the continuous variable that contains the plotted values. With the X() function, that variable name is the first parameter value passed to the function. In this example, the only parameter value passed to the function is the variable name. The data frame is named d, the default value. The following illustrates the call to X() with a continuous variable named \(x\).

To illustrate, consider the continuous variable Salary in the Employee data table. Use X() to tabulate and display the number of employees in each department, here relying upon the default data frame (table) named d, so the data= parameter is not needed.

X(Salary)
## [Interactive plot from the Plotly R package (Sievert, 2020)]

Histogram of tablulated counts for the bins of Salary. 

## >>> Suggestions 
## bin_width: set the width of each bin 
## bin_start: set the start of the first bin 
## bin_end: set the end of the last bin 
## X(Salary, form="density")  # smoothed curve + histogram 
## X(Salary, form="vbs")  # Violin/Box/Scatterplot (VBS) plot 
## 
## --- Salary: Annual Salary (USD) --- 
##  
##     n   miss         mean           sd          min          mdn          max 
##      37      0    83795.557    21799.533    56124.970    79547.600   144419.230 
##  
## 
##   
## --- Outliers ---     from the boxplot: 1 
##  
## Small      Large 
## -----      ----- 
##             144419.2 
## 
## 
## Bin Width: 10000 
## Number of Bins: 10 
##  
##              Bin  Midpnt  Count    Prop  Cumul.c  Cumul.p 
## --------------------------------------------------------- 
##   50000 >  60000   55000      4    0.11        4     0.11 
##   60000 >  70000   65000      8    0.22       12     0.32 
##   70000 >  80000   75000      8    0.22       20     0.54 
##   80000 >  90000   85000      5    0.14       25     0.68

##  100000 > 110000  105000      5    0.14       33     0.89

By default, the X() function provides a color theme according to the current, active theme. The function also provides the corresponding frequency distribution, summary statistics, the table that lists the count of each category, from which the histogram is constructed, as well as an outlier analysis based on Tukey’s outlier detection rules for boxplots.

Customize the Histogram

style(quiet=TRUE)

Use the parameters bin_start, bin_width, and bin_end to customize the histogram.

X(Salary, bin_start=35000, bin_width=14000)

Customized histogram.

Easy to change the color, either by changing the color theme with style(), or just change the fill color with fill. Can refer to standard R colors, as shown with lessR function showColors(), or implicitly invoke the lessR color palette generating function getColors(). Each 30 degrees of the color wheel is named, such as "greens", "rusts", etc, and implements a sequential color palette.

Use the color parameter to set the border color, here turned off.

X(Salary, fill="reds", color="transparent")

Customized histogram.

The default for formatting both axis labels is to round numeric values of thousands, such as 100000 to 100K. With parameter axis_fmt, this default of to {"K"} can be changed. Also can specify {","} to insert commas in large numbers with a decimal point or {"."} to insert periods, or {""} to turn off formatting. The value of {"K"} can also be combined with {","} or {"."} by forming a vector of values, such as c("K", ",").

Axis labels can also formatted by adding a prefix to a numeric value with the parameter axis_pre, such as $ or €. The value of axis_pre can be multiple characters, such as for the Brazilian currency, R$.

X(Salary, axis_fmt=",", axis_x_pre="$")

Formatted axis values.

Frequency Polygon and Proportions

The frequency polygon displays the same binned counts as the histogram, but marks the count of each bin with a point at the bin’s midpoint and connects the points with line segments.

X(Salary, form="freq_poly")

Frequency polygon.

By default the height of each bar, or point, is the count of the values in the bin. Set stat="proportion" to plot the proportion of all the values in each bin instead, so the heights sum to 1. The shape of the distribution is unchanged, but the vertical scale no longer depends on the sample size, which makes the distributions from samples of different sizes comparable.

X(Salary, stat="proportion")

Histogram of proportions.

The parameter stat applies to the forms that plot a frequency, the histogram and the frequency polygon. The other forms, such as the density curve and the VBS plot, do not plot a frequency, so for them stat is not available.

Set cumulate="on" for a cumulative histogram, in which the height of each bar is the count of the values in that bin and all the bins below it. Set cumulate="both" to superimpose the standard histogram on the cumulative histogram.

X(Salary, cumulate="both")

Cumulative histogram with the standard histogram superimposed.

The frequency table at the console then also lists the cumulative counts and cumulative proportions.

Density Plot

The histogram portrays a continuous distribution with discrete bins, with more modern visualizations available that directly display the estimated underlying smooth curve.

Density plot: A smooth curve that estimates the underlying continuous distribution.

To create a density plot, specify the value of form as "density" parameter. The result is the filled density curve superimposed on the histogram.

X(Salary, form="density")

Histogram with density plot.

The kind parameter indicates the type of density curve. The default is "general", which follows the shape of the data. Options are "normal" for the normal density curve with the same mean and standard deviation as the data, and "both" for both. Plotting both curves compares the distribution of the data to a normal distribution, here showing that the distribution of Salary is skewed to the right, with a longer tail at the high salaries than a normal curve would have.

X(Salary, form="density", kind="both")

General and normal density curves.

With a by variable, the density curves of the groups are overlaid in one panel, one curve for each level of by in its own color. With kind="normal", a normal curve is fit to each group separately, with that group’s own mean and standard deviation.

X(Salary, by=Gender, form="density", kind="normal")
## Salary by Gender 
## 
##  Gender  n na     Mean   Median       SD      IQR      Min      Max
##       M 18  0 91147.46 89792.95 23128.44 27772.74 59188.96 144419.2
##       W 19  0 76830.60 71356.69 18438.46 15766.48 56124.97 132563.4
## 
## For inferential analysis of the mean difference:
## > ttest(Salary ~ Gender)

The display of the groups is interactive, drawn with the plotly package. When knitting an R Markdown document, which writes static graphics, assign the result of the function call to an object and then display it, as in p <- X(Salary, by=Gender, form="density"); p.

VBS Plot

A more modern version of the density plot combines the violin plot, boxplot, and scatter plot into a single visualization, here called the VBS plot.

X(Salary, form="vbs")

VBS plot.

The VBS plot is built from three layers, each named by a letter:

  • v: the violin plot, a density curve and its mirror image, which shows the shape of the distribution
  • b: the boxplot, which shows the median, the quartiles, and potential outliers
  • s: the strip plot, a scatterplot of the individual data values, jittered so that nearby values do not overlap

Specify any one layer or any combination of layers with form, the letters given in any order and in either case. For example, form="b" plots the boxplot alone, and form="vs", the violin plot with the individual data values but without the boxplot.

X(Salary, form="vs")

Violin plot with the strip plot.

Each form that includes the strip layer can show the groups of a by variable, each group in its own color. The VBS forms also report summary statistics, which are computed from the data values as read, not from the jittered points, so they are exact and the same on every run. Assign the result of the function call to an object to save the statistics, which are returned as out_pivot, a table of the statistics for each level of the by variable, here Gender.

r <- X(Salary, by=Gender, form="vbs")

r$out_pivot
## Gender   n      Mean    Median        SD       IQR       Min        Max
##      M  18  91147.46  89792.95  23128.44  27772.74  59188.96  144419.23
##      W  19  76830.60  71356.69  18438.46  15766.48  56124.97  132563.38

The men have the higher salaries, with a mean of $91,147 and a median of $89,793, compared with a mean of $76,831 and a median of $71,357 for the women.

Stratification

to visualize the distribution of a continuous variable, such as Salary, grouped by a categorical variable, use the function X() applied to the continuous variable with by or facet arguments for the categorical variable, such as Dept. Better differentiation of the distribution of Salary across the different groups follows from using facet. The example below shows a scatterplot of Salary for each level of Dept.

X(Salary, facet=Dept, form="strip")

The two parameters occupy different channels, so both apply at once: by overlays the groups within a panel and facet places the panels. Each panel of the following histogram carries one distribution per level of Gender, drawn partly transparent so that neither hides the other, with all panels sharing one set of bins.

X(Salary, by=Gender, facet=Dept)

The same composition applies to the density curve and to the frequency polygon.

X(Salary, by=Gender, facet=Dept, form="density")

Not every form overlays. The violin plot, the boxplot, and their composite form="vb" summarize a distribution across the full width of the panel, so one drawn over another is not readable and there is no layer to carry the groups. Those forms take facet alone. The forms that include the strip layer, such as form="vbs", mark the groups on the plotted points.

X(Salary, by=Gender, facet=Dept, form="vbs")

Orientation

As for Chart(), parameter horiz orients the categories. With horiz=TRUE, the categories run down the vertical axis, so the bars, boxes, or curves extend horizontally. For the violin, box, and strip forms, the categories are the levels of the facet variable, one panel per row by default. Set horiz to FALSE to place the panels side by side on a vertical Salary axis, the familiar layout of boxplots compared across groups.

X(Salary, facet=Dept, form="box", horiz=FALSE)

For the histogram, the categories are the bins, which by default run along the horizontal axis, as do the categories of a bar chart from Chart(). Set horiz to TRUE for bars that extend horizontally from a vertical Salary axis. The frequency polygon and density curve rotate the same way. The axis labels follow their variables, so xlab labels the Salary axis in either orientation.

X(Salary, horiz=TRUE)

Histogram with horizontal bars.

XY() has no horiz parameter. Both of its variables are continuous, so there are no categories to orient. To exchange the axes, exchange x and y.

Interactive Input to Create a Histogram

An interactive visualization lets the user in real time change parameter values to change characteristics of the visualization. To create an interactive histogram of the variable Salary that displays the corresponding parameters, run the function interact() with "X" specified.

interact("X")

The interact() function is not run here because interactivity requires to run directly from the R console.

Full Manual

Use the base R help() function to view the full manual for X(). Simply enter a question mark followed by the name of the function.

?Histogram
